```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
  warning = FALSE, message = FALSE

```

This article covers the functions you use before drawing a diet: a few
descriptive summaries, a prey accumulation curve, the classical frequency of
occurrence, aggregation of rare prey to a stated threshold, and export of a
stomach-by-prey matrix. It runs on the public ICES stomach data that ship with
the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract
distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`),
prepared with the standard set-up used throughout the documentation.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
```

## 1. Describe the sample first

`dv_summary()` gives, for each predator, the number of stomachs and prey
records, the number of distinct prey taxa and the mean number of records per
stomach. Pass `by` to break it down by a covariate.

```{r summary}
s <- dv_summary(prep)
s$total_weight <- round(s$total_weight)
s
```

```{r summary-num, include = FALSE}
s_fam <- dv_summary(prep, rank = "family")
cod_taxa <- s$n_taxa[s$predator_common == "Atlantic cod"]
cod_fam  <- s_fam$n_taxa[s_fam$predator_common == "Atlantic cod"]
mac_taxa <- s$n_taxa[s$predator_common == "Atlantic mackerel"]
```

The sample is very uneven: four predators (mackerel, cod, whiting and plaice)
hold `r round(100 * sum(s$n_stomachs[1:4]) / sum(s$n_stomachs))`% of the
stomachs, and `r sum(s$n_stomachs < 20)` of the `r nrow(s)` predators have
fewer than 20 stomachs. Read every statistic for those last ones as anecdote.

By default a taxon is the finest name reached, so "Decapoda" and
*Crangon crangon* count as two even though the second is a decapod. Read that
count as the number of distinct prey names, not as species richness. Pass
`rank` to count taxa at one stated rank, unidentified records excluded:

```{r summary-rank}
head(dv_summary(prep, rank = "family")[, c("predator_common", "n_stomachs", "n_taxa")], 4)
```

Cod has `r cod_taxa` distinct prey names but `r cod_fam` families. Mackerel,
with the largest number of stomachs, has only `r mac_taxa` prey names: most of
its records are "Unidentified material", "Crustacea", "Pisces" or sandeels
(Ammodytidae).

A table of prey records holds only stomachs that contained something, so it
cannot give the share of empty stomachs. That has to come from the full list of
stomachs examined, which the package ships as `ices_stomachs`:

```{r empty}
# % of sampled stomachs flagged empty
e <- tapply(ices_stomachs$stomach_empty %in% 1, ices_stomachs$predator_common, mean)
round(100 * e[c("Atlantic cod", "Atlantic mackerel", "European plaice", "Whiting")], 1)
```

## 2. Is the diet adequately sampled?

`dv_prey_accumulation()` builds the cumulative prey curve: the number of prey
taxa found against the number of stomachs examined, averaged over random orders
of the stomachs. A curve that levels off means more stomachs would add few new
taxa; a curve still rising means the sample is not yet enough.

Count taxa at one stated rank. With the finest names, a curve rises each time
a new coarse name ("Crustacea", "Decapoda") appears next to the species
already seen, and the rise grows with digestion. Here, family:

```{r accumulation}
four <- c("Atlantic cod", "Atlantic mackerel", "European plaice", "Whiting")
acc <- dv_prey_accumulation(prep, by = spec$predator, rank = "family",
                            permutations = 50, seed = 1)
acc <- acc[acc$predator_common %in% four, ]

plot(NA, xlim = c(0, max(acc$n_stomachs)), ylim = c(0, max(acc$mean_richness)),
     xlab = "Stomachs examined", ylab = "Cumulative prey families",
     main = "Prey accumulation at family rank")
cols <- c("#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728")
for (i in seq_along(four)) {
  a <- acc[acc$predator_common == four[i], ]
  lines(a$n_stomachs, a$mean_richness, col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topleft", legend = four, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

```{r accumulation-tail}
# families gained over the last 100 stomachs of each curve
sapply(split(acc, acc$predator_common), function(a) {
  n <- nrow(a)
  round(a$mean_richness[n] - a$mean_richness[n - 100], 1)
})
```

The cod, whiting and plaice curves are still rising slowly at the full sample
size: the last 100 stomachs add one or two families each. The mackerel curve is
flat, but not because the mackerel diet is well sampled: almost nothing in its
stomachs was identified to family. A flat curve says that more stomachs, read
the same way, would add few new families; it says nothing about what better
identification would add.

Keep `permutations` low while exploring and raise it for a figure. The seed is
used for that call only.

## 3. Frequency of occurrence (%FO)

`dv_build_tree()` gives `pct_occ`, the share of prey records. Shares of records
add up across the ranks, which is what lets them be drawn as a sunburst, but
they are not the frequency of occurrence of the diet literature.
`dv_fo_table()` computes %FO: the share of non-empty stomachs that contain each
taxon, computed separately at each rank, as recommended for comparison between
studies (Buckland et al., 2017).

```{r fo}
fo <- dv_fo_table(prep, rank = "class", by = spec$predator)
head(fo[fo$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ], 6)
```

```{r fo-num, include = FALSE}
fc <- fo[fo$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
fo_mal <- fc$pct_fo[fc$taxon == "Malacostraca"]
fo_tel <- fc$pct_fo[fc$taxon == "Teleostei"]
tree_cod <- dv_build_tree(prep$data[prep$data$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ],
                          prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
rc <- dv_rank_table(tree_cod, "Class")
```

Crustaceans (Malacostraca) occur in `r fo_mal`% of the non-empty cod stomachs
and fish (Teleostei) in `r fo_tel`%. The same classes are
`r round(rc$pct_occ[rc$label == "Malacostraca"], 1)`% and
`r round(rc$pct_occ[rc$label == "Teleostei"], 1)`% of the cod's prey records.
The two quantities answer different questions (how many fish ate it, and how
much of the recorded material it is) and should be reported under their own
names. The column `n_total` is the number of non-empty stomachs in the group:
the denominator of %FO.

%FO does not add up across ranks: a parent's %FO is computed from the stomachs
that contain it, not summed from its children, and the `NA` row (stomachs
holding at least one record not identified to class) overlaps the others.
Leave `rank = NULL` to stack every rank.

## 4. Aggregating rare prey to a stated threshold

By default DietView keeps each record at the deepest rank it reached. To make
the reporting resolution a stated choice, `dv_aggregate_threshold()` moves prey
found in fewer than `threshold` stomachs up to their parent, and repeats up the
hierarchy until every category it reports occurs in at least `threshold`
stomachs.

### Choosing the threshold

The threshold is a judgement, so look at what it costs before you fix it.
`dv_threshold_sweep()` runs the aggregation for several values and reports the
number of categories left and the share of records whose category is coarser
than species:

```{r sweep}
sw <- dv_threshold_sweep(prep, thresholds = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100))
sw
```

```{r sweep-num, include = FALSE}
g <- function(x, col) sw[[col]][sw$threshold == x]
```

The share of records above species is high whatever the threshold
(`r g(5, "pct_coarser")`% at 5 stomachs), because most records were never
identified to species. Raising the threshold from 5 to 20 stomachs halves the
number of categories (`r g(5, "n_categories")` to `r g(20, "n_categories")`)
and moves only `r round(g(20, "pct_coarser") - g(5, "pct_coarser"), 1)` more
percent of the records to a coarser rank; beyond 50 the categories become
broad groups. We use 20 stomachs here: about
`r round(100 * 20 / length(unique(dat$stomach_id)), 1)`% of the
`r format(length(unique(dat$stomach_id)), big.mark = ",")` stomachs, enough for
a category to be compared between the main predators, and a point where the
sweep has removed most of the rare names at little cost. State the value and
the reason in your methods; a different question (a per-predator description,
a rare-prey study) would justify a different one.

### The aggregated data

```{r aggregate}
agg <- dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, threshold = 20)
attr(agg, "aggregation")$n_categories
head(sort(table(agg$data$prey_category), decreasing = TRUE), 12)
table(agg$data$prey_rank, useNA = "ifany")
```

A category named after a taxon that also has retained descendants holds only
the records that stayed at that taxon, and its label ends in "(other)".
"Decapoda (other)" holds the decapods that are not in a retained family, genus
or species of their own: the many records named only "Brachyura", "Caridea"
or "Decapoda", and rare decapods merged into them. Named species such as
*Crangon crangon* (brown shrimp), *Merlangius merlangus* (whiting eaten by
other fish) and *Aphia minuta* (transparent goby) are frequent enough to stay
on their own. The `r format(sum(is.na(agg$data$prey_rank)), big.mark = ",")`
records with no prey placement at all stay unidentified (`NA`).

The result is a `dietview_prep` again: ranks finer than the rank each record
settled at are set to `NA`, so it goes straight back into the usual functions,
and the sunburst then has no category rarer than the threshold.

```{r aggregate-tree}
tree_agg <- dv_build_tree(agg$data[agg$data$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ],
                          agg$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(tree_agg, mode = "occurrence", colors = dv_palette_tree(tree_agg),
            title = "Atlantic cod, prey aggregated to 20 stomachs",
            subtitle = "share of prey records")
```

Two arguments give three ways of counting:

```{r architectures, eval = FALSE}
dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, 20)                      # all predators pooled
dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, 20, min_predators = 2)   # pooled, and in at least 2 predators
dv_aggregate_threshold(prep, 20, scope = "per_predator")
```

The per-predator scope counts stomachs within each predator, so a prey must
reach the threshold in one predator's own stomachs. A prey found in 15 cod and
10 whiting stomachs keeps its category in the pooled tree but is merged upward
in both predator trees. That leaves fewer categories at the same threshold:

```{r sweep-per}
dv_threshold_sweep(prep, thresholds = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 50), scope = "per_predator")
```

DietView stops at the aggregation. If you summarize a statistic across several
thresholds, do it in your own analysis.

## 5. Handing over to multivariate analysis

`dv_matrix()` turns the records into the stomach-by-prey matrix that
ordination, PERMANOVA and compositional regression expect. If you aggregated
first, it uses the `prey_category` column automatically. Pass `rank` to build
the matrix at one rank instead.

```{r matrix}
m <- dv_matrix(agg, currency = "weight")
dim(m)
m[1:3, c("Crangon crangon", "Decapoda (other)", "Chordata (other)", "NA")]
```

One row per stomach (`r format(nrow(m), big.mark = ",")`), one column per
category (`r ncol(m)`, the `NA` column included), summed prey weight in each
cell. The matrix is very sparse: `r round(100 * mean(m == 0), 1)`% of its
cells are zero, which is typical of stomach data and matters for the choice of
distance in the analysis that follows.

`currency` is `"weight"` (summed weight), `"occurrence"` (number of records) or
`"fo"` (presence or absence in each unit). Use `unit` to sum over something
coarser than a stomach, such as a haul (`unit = "haul_id"`). Use
`include_na = FALSE` to drop the unidentified column, and say in your methods
that you did.

```{r downstream, eval = FALSE}
# DietView stops here; the analysis uses other packages
mm <- vegan::decostand(m[rowSums(m) > 0, ], "total")
d  <- vegan::vegdist(mm, "bray")
# vegan::adonis2(d ~ predator_common + region, data = stomach_covariates)
```

## Where this fits

These functions describe and aggregate. DietView does not test hypotheses:
diversity tests, PERMANOVA and dispersion analyses belong to packages built for
them, and `dv_matrix()` is the step that hands your data over.

## References

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish
stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. *Fisheries Research*,
196, 126–140.

ICES Stomach Content Database. ICES, Copenhagen. <https://stomachdata.ices.dk>.
Extract distributed with the R package stomachr (Lindmark 2026,
<https://github.com/maxlindmark/stomachr>).
